evidence: src/infrastructure/http/middleware/errorHandler.ts: notFoundHandler and errorHandler (ErrorRequestHandler) map classifyError results to statuses through STATUS_BY_KIND, the only place that mapping exists.

src/infrastructure/http/middleware/staffAuth.ts: requireStaff(staffApiKey) returns a RequestHandler that checks STAFF_KEY_HEADER with timingSafeEqual over SHA-256 digests. The authentication rule lives only here.
Both files export Express middleware with the same style and are used together only by src/infrastructure/http/createHttpApp.ts.

Minor: the error body { error: { code, message } } is built inline in notFoundHandler, errorHandler (BAD_REQUEST branch and classified branch) and requireStaff (UNAUTHORIZED) instead of through a shared helper. This is response-format repetition, not a duplicated domain invariant.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files are Express middleware for one concern: guarding and shaping HTTP request/response handling. errorHandler.ts turns unmatched routes and thrown errors into HTTP responses: notFoundHandler and errorHandler map ErrorKind to status codes through STATUS_BY_KIND, and clientHttpStatus handles errors raised by Express itself. staffAuth.ts does request authentication with requireStaff and STAFF_KEY_HEADER. The two files are used the same way, as RequestHandler/ErrorRequestHandler values wired up in createHttpApp.ts. Neither file bypasses the other's logic, and no business rule appears in both. Each rule has one home: the kind-to-status mapping is only in errorHandler.ts, and the staff-key check is only in staffAuth.ts. The one weak spot is that the error body shape { error: { code, message } } is written inline in notFoundHandler, twice in errorHandler, and in requireStaff, with no shared helper. That is minor repetition of a response format, not a split concern or a bypassed abstraction. A 401 from requireStaff is also a reasonable short-circuit, because authentication rejection is not an application error kind that classifyError would handle. On balance the module is cohesive.
